single: Choose a calendar date, a clock time, or both. The same picker offers all necessary date and time configurations. Additionally, you can use manual input for dates. In time section minute and second steps can be configured. The hour-cycle setting changes how time is displayed. These examples below show how each mode shapes the calendar's user interface.
ranges: A range keeps two endpoints in one selection: two dates, two times, or two dates with times. Use it for a booking period or an opening-hours window. Calendar selection and manual editing share the same validation. If end datetime endpoint is prior to the start endpoint, the calendar will invert them automatically.
presentations: Keep a picker inline when choosing a date is the main task, open a dialog when it needs its own space, or attach an overlay to an input in a form. These presentations share selection and validation inputs, but differ in when edits commit. Inline and native dialog support come with the picker; the anchored overlay uses the optional Angular CDK integration.
localization: Locale affects how people read dates and times: labels, digits, week starts, clock format, and reading direction can all change. Translated controls come from a separate catalog, and a calendar adapter determines which calendar is displayed. The examples combine these settings so you can compare them. Their selected values still use the same Gregorian UTC format.
calendars: A day can have different names without becoming a different day. WKLY keeps consecutive weeks underneath the calendar and lets an adapter supply dates, month names, and conversion rules. Here, selecting a day in the Gregorian, Hebrew, or civil Hijri picker updates its companions. The Gregorian adapter is published; the other two are source examples.
validation: A typed value is not necessarily a usable selection. WKLY keeps invalid edits in a draft, reports the reason, and retains the last committed value until the edit passes validation. Bounds, disabled dates and times, and range rules also apply to calendar actions. The examples expose those errors and Angular form state, including what happens when a required value is cleared.
virtualization: Weeks continue across month and year boundaries, so scrolling can follow the days without replacing a whole month at each step. WKLY uses that sequence for navigation and lets the viewport decide how much of it to show. Compare a month, a month with surrounding weeks, and four fixed rows below, then try jumping to a distant date.
styling: CSS custom properties set the picker's colors and dimensions without changing its selection behavior. Use them to match an existing interface or give a calendar more room. The examples vary the accent, surface colors, and size multiplier; the dark example also shows validation colors. Inline pickers can be styled locally, while dynamically created dialogs and overlays need styles that reach their picker elements.
